{{Short description|Weather-forecasting technique}}
In [[weather forecasting]], '''model output statistics''' ('''MOS''') is a multiple [[linear regression]] technique in which [[wikt:predictand|predictands]], often near-surface quantities (such as two-meter-above-ground-level air [[temperature]], horizontal [[visibility]], and [[wind]] [[Wind direction|direction]], [[Wind speed|speed]] and [[Wind gust|gusts]]), are related statistically to one or more predictors. The predictors are typically forecasts from a [[numerical weather prediction]] (NWP) model, climatic data, and, if applicable, recent surface observations. Thus, output from NWP models can be transformed by the MOS technique into sensible weather parameters that are familiar to a layperson.

==Background==
Output directly from the NWP model's lowest layer(s) generally is not used by forecasters because the actual physical processes that occur within the Earth's [[Planetary boundary layer|boundary layer]] are crudely approximated in the model (i.e., [[Numerical weather prediction#Parameterization|physical parameterizations]]) along with its relatively coarse horizontal resolution. Because of this lack of fidelity and its imperfect initial state, forecasts of near-surface quantities obtained directly from the model are subject to systematic (bias) and random model errors, which tend to grow with time.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lorenz|first1=Edward N.|title=Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow|journal=Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences|date=March 1963|volume=20|issue=2|pages=130–141|doi=10.1175/1520-0469(1963)020<0130:DNF>2.0.CO;2|bibcode = 1963JAtS...20..130L |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Simmons|first1=A.J.|last2=Mureau|first2=R.|last3=Petroliagis|first3=T.|title=Error growth estimates of predictability from the ECMWF forecasting system|journal=Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc.|date=1995|volume=121|issue=527|pages=1739–1771|doi=10.1002/qj.49712152711|bibcode=1995QJRMS.121.1739S }}</ref>

In the development of MOS equations, past observations and archived NWP model forecast fields are used with a screening regression to determine the 'best' predictors and their coefficients for a particular predictand and forecast time. By using archived model forecast output along with verifying surface observations, the resulting equations implicitly take into account physical effects and processes which the underlying numerical weather prediction model cannot explicitly resolve, resulting in much better forecasts of sensible weather quantities. In addition to correcting systematic errors, MOS can produce reliable probabilities of weather events from a single model run. In contrast, despite the enormous amount of computing resources devoted to generating them, ensemble model forecasts' relative frequency of events—often used as a proxy for probability—do not exhibit useful reliability.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rudack|first1=David|last2=Ghirardelli|first2=Judy|title=A Comparative Verification of Localized Aviation Model Output Statistics Program (LAMP) and Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) Model Forecast of Ceiling Height and Visibility|journal=Weather and Forecasting|date=August 2010|volume=25|issue=4|pages=1161–1178|doi=10.1175/2010WAF2222383.1|bibcode = 2010WtFor..25.1161R |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1234555|doi-access=free}}</ref> Thus, ensemble NWP model output also requires additional post-processing in order to obtain reliable probabilistic forecasts, using [[nonhomogeneous Gaussian regression]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Jewson|first1=S.|last2=Brix|first2=A.|last3=Ziehmann|first3=C.|title=A new parametric model for the assessment and calibration of medium-range ensemble temperature forecasts|journal=Atmospheric Science Letters|date=2004|volume=5|issue=5|pages=96–102|doi=10.1002/asl.69|arxiv=physics/0308057|bibcode=2004AtScL...5...96J }}</ref> or other methods.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wilks|first1=Daniel S.|last2=Hamill|first2=Thomas M.|title=Comparison of Ensemble-MOS Methods Using GFS Reforecasts|journal=Monthly Weather Review|date=June 2007|volume=135|issue=6|pages=2379–2390|doi=10.1175/MWR3402.1|bibcode = 2007MWRv..135.2379W |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Veehuis|first1=Bruce|title=Spread Calibration of Ensemble MOS Forecasts.|journal=Monthly Weather Review|date=July 2013|volume=141|issue=7|pages=2467–2482|doi=10.1175/MWR-D-12-00191.1|bibcode=2013MWRv..141.2467V|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1234611|doi-access=free}}</ref><!-- ref>{{cite journal|last1=Glahn|first1=Bob|title=MOS Uncertainty Estimates in an Ensemble Framework.|journal=Monthly Weather Review|date=January 2009|volume=137|issue=1|pages=246–268|doi=10.1175/2008MWR2569.1|bibcode = 2009MWRv..137..246G }}</ref -->

==History==

===United States===
MOS was conceived and planning for its use began within the U.S. [[National Weather Service]]’s (NWS’s) Techniques Development Laboratory (TDL) in 1965 and forecasts first issued from it in 1968.<!-- ref>{{cite journal|last1=Glahn|first1=Harry R.|last2=Lowry|first2=Dale A.|title=The Use of Model Output Statistics (MOS) in Objective Weather Forecasting|journal=Journal of Applied Meteorology and Climatology|date=December 1972|volume=11|issue=8|pages=1203-1211|doi=10.1175/1520-0450(1972)011<1203:TUOMOS>2.0.CO;2|bibcode = 1972JApMe..11.1203G }}</ref --><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Glahn|first1=Harry R.|last2=Dallavalle|first2=J. Paul|title=TDL Office Note 00-1:MOS-2000|journal=Internal Publication|date=January 2000|page=179|url=http://www.mdl.nws.noaa.gov/~qa/pdf_files/TDL_Office_Note_00-1.pdf|accessdate=9 August 2014|publisher=Techniques Development Laboratory|location=Silver Spring Maryland USA|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812115518/http://www.mdl.nws.noaa.gov/~qa/pdf_files/TDL_Office_Note_00-1.pdf|archive-date=12 August 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> Since then, TDL, now the Meteorological Development Laboratory (MDL), continued to create, refine and update MOS equation sets as additional NWP models were developed and made operational at the National Meteorological Center (NMC) and then the [[Environmental Modeling Center]] or EMC.<ref name=Carter>{{cite journal|last1=Carter|first1=Gary M.|last2=Dallevalle|first2=J. Paul|last3=Glahn|first3=Harry R.|title=Statistical Forecasts Based on the National Meteorological Center's Numerical Weather Prediction System|journal=Weather and Forecasting|date=September 1989|volume=4|issue=3|pages=401–412|doi=10.1175/1520-0434(1989)004<0401:SFBOTN>2.0.CO;2|bibcode = 1989WtFor...4..401C |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Given its multi-decadal history within the U.S. NWS and its continuous improvement and superior skill over direct NWP model output, MOS guidance is still used by forecasters within the agency.<ref>{{cite web|author=Unpublished|title=Annual MDL Users Survey 2011|url=http://www.nws.noaa.gov/mdl/survey/2011/results/MDL_Survey_2011_FINAL.pdf|accessdate=3 August 2014|pages=25–27}}</ref>

==United States forecast guidance==

There are eight sets of MOS guidance available from MDL, operational and experimental, covering the span of time from the next hour out to ten days for the United States and most of its territories.<ref group=note>[[Guam]] and surrounding [[Northern Mariana Islands]] only have GFS MOS guidance available</ref>

[[Nested Grid Model]] MOS was discontinued in 2009.<ref>[https://www.weather.gov/mdl/mos_changelog MOS changelog]. Retrieved May 12, 2019.</ref>

Initially, MOS guidance was developed for airports and other fixed locales where [[METAR]]s (or similar reports) were routinely issued. Therefore, MOS guidance was and continues to be provided in an alphanumeric 'bulletin' format for these locations. Here is an example of a short-range MOS forecast for Clinton-Sherman Airport, Oklahoma (KCSM) based on the EMC's [[Global Forecast System]] model output.

With the availability of private- and government-owned weather [[mesonet]]s,<ref>{{cite web|last1=NOAA|first1=Earth Systems Research Laboratory|url=http://madis.noaa.gov/network_info.html|title=MADIS Surface Network Information|accessdate=7 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812120033/http://madis.noaa.gov/network_info.html|archive-date=12 August 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> new objective analysis and interpolation techniques,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Glahn|first1=Bob|last2=Im|first2=J.S.|title=Algorithms for effective objective analysis of surface weather variables|journal=24th Conf. ===Advantages and disadvantages===
The advantage of MOS forecast guidance as developed in the United States allowed for
* the removal of NWP model bias,
* prediction of [[weather]] elements not forecast by the NWP model, e.g., surface visibilities, [[Ceiling (cloud)|cloud ceiling]] heights,
* reliable probabilities of binary events, e.g. [[probability of precipitation]] and (severe) [[thunderstorm]]s,
* reliable probabilities of categorical events, e.g., probability of clear, scattered, broken or [[overcast]] skies.

These points, while greatly desired by forecasters, do come at a price. From its very beginnings, the development of robust MOS equations for a particular NWP model required at least two years' worth of archived model output and observations, during which time the NWP model should remain unchanged, or nearly so. This requirement is necessary in order to fully capture the model's error characteristics under a wide variety of meteorological flow regimes for any particular location or region. Extreme meteorological events such as unusual cold- or heat-waves, heavy rain and snowfall, high winds, etc., are important in the development of robust MOS equations. A lengthy model archive has the best chance of capturing such events.

From the 1970s and into the 1980s, this requirement was not very onerous since [[Environmental Modeling Center|EMC]] (then NMC) scientists, being relatively constrained by computational resources at the time, could only make relatively minor, incremental improvements to their NWP models. However, since the 1990s, NWP models have been upgraded more frequently, oftentimes with significant changes in physics and horizontal and vertical grid resolutions.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Environmental Modeling Center|first1=Mesoscale Modeling Branch|url=http://www.emc.ncep.noaa.gov/NAM/clog.php#TAB4|
title=Mesoscale Branch Web Page Reference List|accessdate=7 August 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Environmental Modeling Center|first1=Global Branch|title=[GFS/GDAS] Changes since 1991|url=http://www.emc.ncep.noaa.gov/gmb/STATS/html/model_changes.html|accessdate=7 August 2014}}</ref> Since MOS corrects systematic biases of the NWP model it is based on, any changes to the NWP model's error characteristics affects MOS guidance, usually in a negative way.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Erickson|first1=Mary C.|title=Evaluating the Impact of RAFS Changes on the NGM-Based MOS Guidance|journal=Weather and Forecasting|date=March 1991|volume=6|issue=1|pages=142–147|doi=10.1175/1520-0434(1991)006<0142:ETIORC>2.0.CO;2|bibcode = 1991WtFor...6..142E |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Erickson|first1=Mary C.|last2=Dallavalle|first2=J. Paul|last3=Carroll|first3=Kevin L.|title=The new AVN/MRF MOS development and model changes: a volatile mix?|journal=16th Conference on Probability and Statistics in the Atmospheric Sciences|date=January 2002|url=https://ams.confex.com/ams/annual2002/techprogram/paper_27642.htm|accessdate=5 August 2014}}</ref> This was a factor in the discontinuation of the MOS for the individual ensemble members of the GFS in April 2019; that product had not been updated since 2009, and NOAA decided to cease offering the product instead of bringing it up to date.<ref>[https://www.weather.gov/media/notification/scn19-23gets_mos_termination.pdf SCN19-23: Termination of the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS)-based Model Output Statistics (MOS) product (MEN) on or about April 16, 2019] Retrieved May 12, 2019</ref>

In the case of a major upgrade to a NWP model, the [[Environmental Modeling Center|EMC]] will run the newer version of model in parallel with the operational one for many months to allow for direct comparison of model performance.<ref>{{cite web|last1=National Centers for Environmental Prediction|first1=Environmental Modeling Center|url=http://www.emc.ncep.noaa.gov/gmb/wd20rt/vsdb/prhw14/www/scorecard/mainindex.html|title=EMC Verification Scorecard|accessdate=12 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812220853/http://www.emc.ncep.noaa.gov/gmb/wd20rt/vsdb/prhw14/www/scorecard/mainindex.html|archive-date=12 August 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> In addition to parallel real-time runs, EMC also runs the newer model to examine past events and seasons, i.e., retrospective forecasts.

All of these runs from the upgraded model allow the National Weather Service, [[Weather Prediction Center]] (WPC), [[National Hurricane Center]] (NHC), and [[Storm Prediction Center]] (SPC) to evaluate its performance prior to the decision to either accept or reject it for operational use. MDL scientists have taken advantage of these runs to evaluate and reformulate the MOS equations as needed to avoid deterioration in guidance quality.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Antolik|first1=Mark|last2=Baker|first2=Michael|title=On the ability to develop MOS guidance with short dependent samples from an evolving numerical model.|journal=23rd Conference Weather Analysis and Forecasting/19th Conference Numerical Prediction|date=2 June 2009|volume=6A.1|url=https://ams.confex.com/ams/pdfpapers/154242.pdf|accessdate=9 August 2014}}</ref>

==Other weather centers==
[[Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute]] developed a MOS system to forecast probabilities of (severe) thunderstorms in the Netherlands.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Schmeits|first1=Maurice J.|last2=Kok|first2=Kees J.|last3=Vogelezang|first3=Daan H. P.|title=Probabilistic Forecasting of (Severe) Thunderstorms in the Netherlands Using Model Output Statistics|journal=Weather and Forecasting|date=April 2005|volume=20|issue=2|pages=134–148|doi=10.1175/WAF840.1|bibcode = 2005WtFor..20..134S |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=van Gastel|first1=Valentijn|title=Investigating MSG-SEVIRI data as an additional predictor source in the KNMI probabilistic (severe) thunderstorm forecasting system|url=http://www.knmi.nl/bibliotheek/knmipubIR/IR2012-01.pdf|website=Koninklijk Nederlands Meteorologisch Instituut|publisher=Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (KNMI) publication|accessdate=9 August 2014}}</ref>

Scientists from the Meteorological Service of Canada developed a post-processing system called Updateable MOS (UMOS) that quickly incorporates changes to their regional NWP model without the need for a lengthy model archive.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wilson|first1=Laurence|last2=Vallee|first2=Marcel|title=The Canadian Updateable Model Output Statistics (UMOS) System: Design and Development Tests|journal=Weather and Forecasting|date=April 2002|volume=17|issue=2|pages=206–222|doi=10.1175/1520-0434(2002)017<0206:TCUMOS>2.0.CO;2|bibcode = 2002WtFor..17..206W |doi-access=free}}</ref> The Canadian UMOS system generates a 2-day forecast of temperatures, wind speed and direction and probability of precipitation (POP). UMOS temperature and wind forecasts are provided at 3-h intervals, and POP at 6-h intervals.

Scientists at the Kongju National University have also implemented a UMOS system to create forecasts of air temperatures over South Korea.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kang|first1=Jeon-Ho|last2=Suh|first2=Myoung-Seok|last3=Hong|first3=Ki-Ok|last4=Kim|first4=Chansoo|title=Development of updateable model output statistics (UMOS) system for air temperature over South Korea|journal=Asia-Pacific Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences|date=February 2011|volume=47|issue=2|pages=199–211|doi=10.1007/s13143-011-0009-8|bibcode = 2011APJAS..47..199K }}</ref> It is unclear as to whether it is used operationally at the Korean Meteorological Administration.
